Chapter 3: Motherhood, Legacy, and the Urgency of Storytelling.
The moment a child arrives, everything shifts. Suddenly, all those big questions—about what really matters, about what we leave behind—become urgent and real. If you’re a new mother, you probably know this feeling: the future isn’t just about you anymore. It’s about what you’ll pass down, and what stories will shape the next little life in your arms.
In those quiet hours—maybe when the world is asleep and you’re holding your baby close—thoughts drift to the stories you want them to grow up with. How do you talk about both the pain and the resilience that made your family who they are? How do you honor the memory of those who suffered, but not pass along the weight of their sorrow? It’s tricky, isn’t it? You want to tell the truth, but you never want that truth to become a cage.
Motherhood has this way of sharpening things, making it clear just how much storytelling matters. She realized that silence—just not talking about the past—can sometimes hurt as much as the past itself. If we don’t share these stories, our kids might be left drifting, searching for answers in all the wrong places. The stories we tell shape not only how they see the world, but how they see themselves.
There were days when the responsibility felt like too much. How do you protect your child from pain, without pretending the pain never happened? How do you show them what strength looks like, without teaching them to be afraid? These questions don’t just go away—they push us to really look at our own family history, and at how we carry it.
Soon, she saw that storytelling isn’t just about sharing facts. It’s about belonging. It’s about helping someone feel connected to something bigger than themselves. Telling her family’s story became an act of reclaiming—of saying, “We were here. We mattered.” Even when others tried to erase those lives, the story says: not so fast.
It’s easy to fall into the habit of thinking we should leave the past behind. But for this mother, the past was always close by—shaping her choices, shaping who she was becoming. The real challenge? Find a way to honor what came before, without getting stuck in it. To pass on a legacy of strength—and not just sorrow.
